tldr: By building "HumanTouch," a 1,000-hour bimanual tactile manipulation dataset, and leveraging touch both as a "spatial teacher for visual tokens during training" and as an "input for action generation," this research significantly boosts dexterous manipulation performance whether tactile sensors are available at runtime or not.
hero_caption: Overall framework of Spark-0. It shows (a) multimodal pretraining including 1,000 hours of human tactile data, (b) the dual roles of touch (spatial alignment training for visual tokens and tactile conditioning for the action expert), (c) the SparkArena evaluation suite combining simulation and real-world setups, and (d) benchmark results significantly outperforming existing baselines.
overview:
In dexterous robot manipulation, contact forces and incipient slip are extremely difficult to observe purely from camera images, and hands frequently occlude the contact areas. While tactile sensors have gained significant traction to tackle this issue, prior work has predominantly treated tactile data merely as an additional input to the model. Using touch as a supervisory signal for large-scale multimodal pretraining has remained largely unexplored.

To address this, the authors developed "Spark-0," a model that divides touch into two complementary roles: a training-only spatial teacher that refines visual features, and a contact dynamics input that directly guides action generation via an Action Expert. To scale this supervision, they collected "HumanTouch," a new 1,000-hour dataset of high-precision bimanual tactile data, finger poses, and multi-view video of human manipulation, enabling large-scale vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) pretraining.

For evaluation, they built "SparkArena," a new benchmark that enables fair comparison between vision-only simulation and tactile-conditioned real-robot tasks on the same hand-arm robot embodiment, and also evaluated on the external humanoid benchmark "Ego Humanoid." Spark-0 achieved the highest success rates across all tracks and aggregate metrics, outperforming existing state-of-the-art baselines.

Most surprisingly, even when deployed without any tactile sensors in a vision-only setup, pretraining with tactile supervision dramatically increased the success rate on Ego Humanoid from 52.5% to 71.7% compared to a model pretrained with touch discarded. This proves that touch is not just an execution-time sensor input, but a powerful supervisory signal that enhances visual representations themselves.
contributions: Constructed "HumanTouch," a large-scale, 1,000-hour bimanual contact-rich manipulation dataset collected with tactile gloves that can be mounted directly onto robot hands.

Proposed "Spark-0," a model that supervises visual tokens with tactile-derived contact maps while feeding tactile dynamics only into the Action Expert, allowing a single checkpoint to support both vision-only and tactile-conditioned deployment.
Released "SparkArena," a benchmark that pairs vision-only simulation tasks with tactile-conditioned real-robot tasks using the same dexterous robot embodiment.
Demonstrated that large-scale tactile pretraining yields significant performance gains even during zero-shot transfer to an unseen robot embodiment without touch sensors at test time.

sections.heading: Why use touch as a pretraining teacher, not just an input?
sections.summary: Even VLA models with extensive visual pretraining struggle with contact-rich dexterous manipulation. This work asks whether touch can serve not only as a policy input, but also as a scalable supervisory signal for refining visual features.
sections.details:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models pretrained on large-scale visual data possess strong semantic understanding and motor priors. However, camera images alone cannot fully capture fingertip contact forces, minute slips, or compliance changes. Moreover, the hand itself constantly occludes the contact points during manipulation.

Conventional approaches have mostly focused on feeding tactile sensor readings into the policy as temporal feedback or predicting latent tactile tokens. However, three major bottlenecks have remained:

- The lack of large-scale, full-hand tactile datasets synchronized with precise finger poses and multi-view video.
- Treating touch solely as an extra policy input rather than a supervisory teacher for pretraining visual representations.
- The absence of a benchmark that consistently evaluates both visual dexterity and contact-rich tactile control.

This led the authors to ask: "Can touch serve as a scalable supervisory signal for dexterous visuomotor pretraining?" To test this hypothesis, they collected 1,000 hours of human tactile data in "HumanTouch" and developed the "Spark-0" model along with the "SparkArena" evaluation suite.

sections.heading: Limitations of prior work and where Spark-0 stands
sections.summary: Tactile datasets, dexterous manipulation policies, and robotics benchmarks have advanced rapidly. However, a major gap remains in terms of data scale, synchronization precision, and the concept of using touch to pretrain visual representations.
sections.details:
### Status of Tactile Datasets
Tactile sensors range from local high-resolution sensors like GelSight and DIGIT to flexible sensor arrays that cover the entire hand. However, existing datasets are either limited in scale or lack millisecond-level synchronization with finger kinematics and multi-view camera feeds. HumanTouch stands out with its 1,000-hour scale, and the fact that the same gloves used for data collection can be worn directly by robot hands.

### Contact-Rich Dexterous Manipulation Policies
Combining VLA models with action diffusion or flow matching is progressing rapidly. Yet, most tactile manipulation research treats touch merely as action conditioning or feedback. For instance, recent works like STAR use around 200 hours of robot data to handle tactile sparsity. Spark-0 sets itself apart by combining heterogeneous data with 1,000 hours of human touch to directly supervise visual tokens through spatial alignment.

### Manipulation Benchmarks
Recent benchmarks focus primarily on parallel-jaw gripper long-horizon tasks or simulation environments. Standardized platforms that rigorously evaluate multi-fingered dexterous hands and tactile sensing on real hardware are exceedingly rare. SparkArena was created to seamlessly evaluate and contrast vision-only simulation and tactile-conditioned real-robot tasks on the exact same robotic embodiment.

sections.heading: The 1,000-hour "HumanTouch" dataset and pretraining data recipe
sections.summary: HumanTouch records natural contact-rich tasks across 32 operators, fully synchronized at 60Hz. Spark-0 pretrains on a heterogeneous mix of HumanTouch, egocentric video, real robot data, and simulation.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Data Collection Hardware
The hardware setup consists of bimanual piezoresistive flexible tactile gloves with 460 sensing points per hand, a 25-joint finger motion capture system, wrist trackers, a head camera, and two wrist cameras, all synchronized at 60Hz. To prevent structural false-positive pressure artifacts caused by bending finger joints, 140 points in bending areas are discarded, leaving 320 taxels per hand as valid observations.

### 3.2 Dataset Scale and Diversity
HumanTouch encompasses over 100 contact-rich real-world tasks performed by 32 operators, totaling 1,000 hours. Rather than repetitive trajectories, it captures diverse object materials, contact patterns, motion complexities, and episode durations.

### 3.3 Pretraining Data Recipe
Each data source in Spark-0's pretraining has a dedicated role:
- **HumanTouch (35%)**: Provides direct supervision of full-hand contact from humans.
- **EgoDex (39%)**: Covers diverse scenes, objects, and motions from egocentric video.
- **Real robot data with the same glove (9%)**: Directly aligns robot morphology and contact signals.
- **Real robot data without touch (5%)**: Enhances visual control in physical robot environments.
- **Simulation data (5%)**: Adds visual diversity via domain randomization.
- **Other robot datasets (Fourier ActionNet 4%, AgiBot World 3%)**: Expands overall robot task diversity.

captions.P3: Figure 2: Overview of the HumanTouch dataset. It captures diverse contact-rich tasks with everyday objects, tools, and containers in natural operating environments.

sections.heading: Architecture design: Giving touch two complementary roles
sections.summary: Spark-0 decouples touch into spatial supervision for visual tokens and contact dynamics conditioning for the Action Expert. Because raw tactile values do not enter the vision-language backbone, a single checkpoint supports both vision-only and tactile-conditioned deployment.
sections.details:
### 4.1 VLA Backbone and Unified Action Space
The base model uses Qwen3-VL-4B coupled with a flow-matching-based Action Expert (DiT structure). To handle morphological and coordinate discrepancies between humans and robots, all data are converted offline into a unified action space (58 dimensions total for both hands) comprising 20 joint angles and end-effector SE(3) poses on the target robot hand (WUJI Hand 2). Everything is referenced to the head-camera frame to align visual and action coordinates.

### 4.2 Spatial Alignment: Teaching vision where contact occurs
Visual tokens at layer 25 of the VLM are supervised with two training-only auxiliary losses. Both auxiliary heads are discarded at inference:
- **Geometry Alignment**: Aligns VLM tokens with features from a pretrained Depth-Anything-3 (DA3) teacher using cosine similarity to encode scene-level 3D geometry.
- **Contact Alignment**: Computes contact intensity across a 3D hand mesh (MANO model) using tactile values from the gloves, and projects it into a 2D contact map in the head-camera frame. Visual tokens predict this map as a soft target trained with Focal and Dice losses. This allows the model to internally infer which parts of the hand are contacting an object purely from camera images.

### 4.3 Tactile Fusion: Injecting contact dynamics into action generation
To capture force changes and slip that cannot be observed from images alone, a dedicated tactile encoder connects directly to the Action Expert (DiT):
- **Regional Force Histories**: Groups 6 anatomical hand regions over the last 20 frames (~333ms) and aggregates force changes using temporal convolutions to output 12 tokens.
- **3D Taxel States**: Processes current 3D positions and pressures of active taxels with a Point MLP and attention pooling to yield 12 3D tokens.

These 24 tactile tokens are concatenated with state tokens (3 tokens) and action tokens (50 tokens) and processed via masked joint self-attention inside the DiT. If tactile sensors are unavailable, they are replaced with learnable placeholder tokens, preventing the policy from failing during vision-only deployment.

captions.P4: Figure 3: Spark-0 model architecture. (a) Coupling of the VLM and Action Expert, (b) DiT blocks that attend to VLM features in even layers and perform joint self-attention over state, touch, and action in odd layers, (c) Tactile encoder, and (d) Asymmetric attention mask restricting attention from tactile queries.

sections.heading: SparkArena: A new sim-and-real benchmark on a single embodiment
sections.summary: To evaluate tactile pretraining, the authors created SparkArena on the "Gen 1 Prototype" bimanual dexterous robot. It consists of 7 vision-only simulation tasks and 5 tactile-conditioned real-robot tasks.
sections.details:
### Evaluation Goals
Rigorous evaluation of tactile pretraining requires measuring two distinct properties on the same robotic embodiment: how much the visual policy improves when deployed without touch, and how stable contact control becomes when online touch is available. Existing benchmarks could not satisfy both criteria, motivating the development of SparkArena.

### SparkArena-Sim (Simulation Track)
A vision-only track testing dexterity and long-horizon planning across 7 tasks:
- Click Mouse
- Collect Objects
- Dual Bottles Pick
- Hammer Beat
- Put Food in Microwave
- Retrieve Gap
- Stack Bowls

### SparkArena-Real (Real-Robot Track)
Equipped with Moxian tactile gloves, the robot tackles 5 difficult contact-rich tasks where contact states are hard to observe visually: Insert Test Tubes, Pack Shoes into Box, Place the Phone, Stack Bowls, and Stand Up Bottle. To ensure fair evaluation, all policies are tested from strictly standardized initial states.

captions.P7: Figure 4: The 7 tasks in SparkArena-Sim. They span dexterous challenges unique to multi-fingered hands, including tool use, precision fingertip control, bimanual coordination, and narrow-gap retrieval.

sections.heading: Experimental results: Massive gains from tactile pretraining
sections.summary: Spark-0 achieved first place across all tracks in SparkArena and all 8 aggregate metrics on Ego Humanoid. Ablation studies prove that supervising visual tokens with 1,000 hours of touch dramatically boosts zero-shot transfer to unseen robots without touch.
sections.details:
### 6.1 Vision-Only Control Performance (SparkArena-Sim & Ego Humanoid)
In SparkArena-Sim without tactile sensing, Spark-0 achieved a mean success rate of 36.86%, outperforming the strongest baseline FastWAM (28.29%) by 8.57 points. It substantially outperformed generalist robot VLA models like GR00T-N1.7 (14.00%) and RDT-1B (9.71%).

On the external "Ego Humanoid" benchmark with an unseen embodiment, Spark-0 led across all metrics. The gain was especially pronounced in long-horizon tasks, where Spark-0 scored 61.82% in unseen environments—a 22.12-point margin over the strongest baseline, VITRA (39.70%).

### 6.2 Real-Robot Contact-Rich Control (SparkArena-Real)
With online tactile feedback in SparkArena-Real, Spark-0 achieved a 52.00% success rate and a completion score of 62.80, leading the tactile foundation model FTP-1 (36.00% / 47.80) by 16.00 points. Vision-only baselines (π0.5, GR00T) often made initial contact but failed during delicate insertion or force adjustment, languishing in the 10% range.

### 6.3 Tactile Pretraining Ablation and Scaling Laws
To isolate what touch during pretraining contributes, four variants were evaluated:
- **Scratch**: No pretraining.
- **Visual PT**: Pretrained on the same RGB data and compute as 1000H, but with tactile signals completely discarded.
- **100H**: Retaining touch from 100 hours of HumanTouch.
- **1000H (Spark-0)**: Retaining all touch from 1,000 hours of HumanTouch.

On Ego Humanoid (deployed without touch sensors), Visual PT achieved only a 52.45% success rate. Adding tactile supervision on the exact same visual data in 1000H boosted success to **71.72%**—a massive 19.27-point leap. Scaling tactile data from 100 to 1,000 hours also demonstrated consistent performance gains, confirming clear scaling behavior.

captions.P8: Table 1: Success rates and completion scores across tasks in SparkArena-Sim. Spark-0 secures top scores (highlighted in blue) on most tasks and significantly outpaces existing models in average success rate.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Turning touch from a policy input into a pretraining teacher
sections.summary: Spark-0 sets a new standard for dexterous manipulation by using touch both as a spatial pretraining teacher and as dynamic conditioning for actions. Scaling tactile data offers a clear path toward enhancing the generalization of visual policies themselves.
sections.details:
This work presented the spatially aligned VTLA model "Spark-0," the 1,000-hour bimanual tactile dataset "HumanTouch," and the unified sim-and-real evaluation suite "SparkArena."

The key finding is that visual tokens pretrained with tactile supervision generalize remarkably well to unseen environments and new robot embodiments, even when no tactile sensors are available at test time. This demonstrates that touch is far more than just execution-time sensory feedback; it is a scalable pretraining signal that helps models visually comprehend physical interaction. This study highlights tactile data collection and integration as an indispensable pillar for future robot foundation models.

takeaways: Using touch as a training-only spatial teacher (contact maps) rather than just an execution-time input dramatically enhances the policy's ability to infer contact points directly from images.
Even when deployed in vision-only tasks without touch sensors, pretraining with tactile data substantially improves zero-shot transfer to unseen humanoid robots (from 52.5% to 71.7%).
The benefits of tactile pretraining do not saturate at 100 hours; scaling up to 1,000 hours is crucial to unlocking its full potential.
Collecting human data with tactile gloves that can also be directly mounted onto robot hands is a practical and scalable approach for physical skill transfer from humans to robots.
limitations: In tasks requiring sub-millimeter clearances, such as the Insert Test Tubes task, the success rate remains at 0%, showing improvements only in partial completion scores.
Because joint-bending regions on the tactile glove produce false-positive pressure artifacts, 140 taxels had to be masked out, ignoring contact in those specific flexed areas.
While self-occlusion by the hand is addressed during contact map rendering, accurately rendering contact points when the hand is fully occluded by grasped objects remains an open challenge.
